title: Behar: strangers and settlers (Leviticus 25:23)
hookLine: the land is God's, "for ye are strangers and settlers with Me"

lines: A DEED, A LEASE, A FENCE.
cards: Somewhere there's a deed with your family's name on it, or a lease, or at least a parking spot you think of as yours. A fence, a title, a signature at a closing table with too many pens.

The Torah has paperwork too: fields are bought and sold in Leviticus, with prices worked out by the year. Then, in the middle of all those transactions, God says something that turns every deed into a rental agreement.
The field you just paid for was never really for sale.

teach.b: This week's portion is called Behar, on the mountain, because it opens at Sinai. You've met the rest year and the jubilee, when land goes home to the family that first held it.
Here is the reason the Torah gives, in Leviticus twenty-five, verse twenty-three: "And the land shall not be sold in perpetuity; for the land is Mine; for ye are strangers and settlers with Me."
In Hebrew, gerim v'toshavim. The ger came up three days ago, at one law for all: someone living in a place that isn't originally theirs. A toshav is a settler, someone staying on.
Together they make a careful picture: you really live here, you plant and harvest and raise children here, and still, you're a guest. Notice the last word: with Me.
Not strangers to God; strangers alongside God, sharing the house with its owner. The same pairing turns up elsewhere.

Abraham, buying a burial cave for Sarah, introduces himself to the Hittites as a stranger and a sojourner. A psalm asks God to hear, because the singer is a stranger with God, a sojourner, as all their ancestors were.
So the law does two things at once. It protects the poor family that had to sell, because the land comes back.
And it reminds the wealthy buyer that they hold a lease, not a crown.
Some readers hear a check on pride in it: if even the land is borrowed, so is much of what a person holds.

how: Behar is read in synagogue in the spring, often paired with Bechukotai. In the Land of Israel some farmers still let fields rest in the seventh year, and the idea that the earth belongs to God shapes Jewish teaching about property and charity.

o: on the mountain, the portion opening at Sinai
a deed of sale for a family's field
the high place where offerings burned

games.q: guests on God's land — tap the pairs.

s: in Leviticus, land sold is gone from the family forever
the land shall not be sold in perpetuity; in the jubilee it goes back.
Abraham called himself a stranger and a sojourner
he said it to the Hittites while buying a burial place for Sarah.
the verse calls Israel strangers to God
it says strangers and settlers with Me: guests alongside God, not apart from God.

games.q: you're a wealthy buyer in ancient Israel. you've just paid for a poor family's field. what does the law say you've bought?
o: the harvests until the jubilee year.
nothing at all; the sale is forbidden.
games.why: the price is set by the years left until the jubilee. you bought a lease on the harvests, because the land itself belongs to God.

practice: Pick up something near you that you'd call yours, a phone, a ring, a key, and open your hand flat so it rests on your palm instead of in your grip.
Think about where it came from, who made it, how long it will outlast you or how soon it won't. You don't have to give it away; just hold it the way a guest holds a borrowed cup.

wordCard.voice: Behar. On the mountain: the portion that says the land rests, the land returns, and everyone on it is a guest of its owner.

orig.note: Hebrew: strangers and settlers. guests who live here, and still guests.

carryVoice: Your line: we are guests here. Guests who stay, and plant, and belong. Day four hundred twenty-two, done.
